Create your account

One form spins up a private slice of the platform

  • Name, email, company, event code → your own private space, instantly
  • One API chain: a private entity, an invited user, an iMX95genai device with an x.509 cert
  • You only ever see your own board — isolation is the platform's, not the UI's

Everything here is the same public REST API a customer uses to onboard a fleet. The success screen ('You're onboarded') confirms the entity and device now exist.

Download your board kit

The kit IS your credentials — a real x.509 device identity

  • Onboarding hands you a board kit (.zip): iotcDeviceConfig.json + x.509 cert + private key
  • Three files — copied onto the board (the claim page does it for you)
  • Plus a console link and your device id (p95…)

The credential-download step. Those three files are exactly what authenticates the board to /IOTCONNECT over mutual-TLS MQTT — the same identity mechanism a production device ships with.

Get your welcome email

The standard platform invite — a one-time password to bootstrap login

  • A one-time temporary password, emailed to you
  • Sign in once at awspoc.iotconnect.io, then set a real one
  • The platform's normal user invite — nothing workshop-specific

Standard /IOTCONNECT invitation flow. The temp password is single-use; first login forces a reset.

Set your password

First login forces a reset — the temp password is single-use

  • Sign in with the temp password; the platform asks you to set your own
  • Your account, dashboard, and RAG documents stay yours
  • The board goes back after the event; the account doesn't
01 · SIGN UP02 · EMAIL03 · PASSWORD04 · CLAIM05 · CONNECTED06 · COCKPIT
Good wrap-up beat: the hardware is borrowed, the /IOTCONNECT entity is theirs to keep.

Claim your board

A page the board serves itself, and a drag-and-drop that installs a real identity

  • Download your board kit (.zip) — config + x.509 cert + key
  • Open the board's own URL from its card — http://imx95-XXXX.local:8088
  • Drag the kit on → identity installs, demo restarts → “✓ Connected”
  • Re-claiming needs explicit confirmation — no accidental board theft
01 · SIGN UP02 · EMAIL03 · PASSWORD04 · CLAIM05 · CONNECTED06 · COCKPIT
The kit is a real production x.509 device identity. The claim page is served locally by the board on port 8088 — no cloud round-trip to install identity.

Watch it come online

The board finds its broker itself and streams — the production pipeline, not a mock

  • The board found its broker and credentials itself at boot
  • Template = the contract: 54 telemetry attributes, 17 commands
  • D2C: ~50 attributes every 10 s over MQTT
  • C2D: every dashboard button is a real command, acknowledged
01 · SIGN UP02 · EMAIL03 · PASSWORD04 · CLAIM05 · CONNECTED06 · COCKPIT
The full hop is laptop -> REST API -> C2D command (MQTT) -> board runs the model -> D2C telemetry -> dashboard. Same pipeline a fleet of thousands uses.

The same /IOTCONNECT account — scoped to your board

  • Log in with the same credentials from your welcome email
  • The platform scopes everything to your entity — you only see your board
  • No new account, no separate password

Voice & RAG, on the board

Four models in a row, and a knowledge base you feed yourself

  • Voice: “Hey NXP” → wake word → STT → LLM → TTS — fully offline
  • RAG: drop a document or index a web page → chunked & embedded on the board
  • Grounded answers quote your own docs, verbatim

RAG is the 'teach the board its own manual' beat — chunked and embedded locally, then retrieved into the prompt. Voice is the finale of the live workshop.

What you leave knowing

Four ideas the whole flow was built to teach

tok/s is a bandwidth story

Every token reads essentially all the weights once — speed is memory-bandwidth-bound.

Quantize, then re-validate

4-bit is survivable with mixed precision, brutal without it.

Ground or agent small models

RAG retrieves real passages; an agent runs a real tool — both beat guessing.

Measure load separately

Load, TTFT and tok/s are three numbers — never bury load in throughput.

Return to these in the wrap-up as “we did all of this.” Board goes back; the /IOTCONNECT account, dashboard, and RAG docs stay theirs.
